Also look for grim_percentage as a named tool - I might need to searc...The paper's statistical claims rest on shaky ground. The core problem is that the survey percentages in Table III are impossible under the printed denominators (n=80 and n=79). Reconstructing the 2x2 tables shows the survey items were answered by only 73–74 trainees per cohort, not the full 159. That means the reported compliance rates (14.86% vs 34.25% daily MVI use, 37.84% vs 63.01% most days) and the p-values tied to them are based on available-case analysis, not the full sample. The paper never flags this discrepancy, and the explicit statement that “all trainees completed questionnaires” directly contradicts the numbers.

The same issue infects the injury analysis. The chi-squared tests treat the two flights as independent clusters, but the methods section reveals the flights were the actual randomization units. With only two clusters per arm, any flight-level clustering (shared barracks stress, training load, instructor effects) inflates the reported significance (MSKI p=.047, BSI p=.037). Those p-values drive the abstract’s 43% and 66% relative risk reductions, so the inference is anti-conservative.

Title and discussion language compounds the problem. The title claims “ Multivitamin Compliance Reduces Injuries,” yet both arms received the identical MVI; the contrast was only briefing modality. The discussion then infers that the briefing improved compliance, which in turn reduced injuries, without mediation analysis or an unsupplemented control. That causal chain is not identified in the data.

Power analysis is also 2–3 orders of magnitude off. The stated calculation (α=0.05, power=0.99, 25% relative increase in compliance) requires hundreds to thousands per arm, not 77. The printed n=77 per cohort is therefore impossible.

Demographic claims contain another contradiction: Table II shows 21±3 vs 23±5 years, yet the text asserts “no significant differences in age.” The t-test on those means yields p=0.0026, so the “no difference” statement is false.

Vitamin C in Table I is listed as 100 μg (83% DV), but NIH values 100 mg is the correct amount for pregnant/lactating women; 100 μg would be 0.08%. The printed value matches the percent only if the absolute is 100 mg, not μg.

Medical-hold percentages are also inconsistent: 1.27% appears in both columns, but 1/80 = 1.25% and only 1/79 = 1.27%. The video-only cell cannot be correct at n=80.

Finally, reference 8 (Martineau et al.) does not estimate iron requirements; the 22 mg figure is unsupported by that citation.

These are not minor transcription slips. 11 findings, mostly severity 3–5, cluster around the same core issues: wrong denominators, invalid analysis of clustered data, over-claimed causality, and factual errors in tables and text. The paper’s main conclusion—that an in-person briefing improved compliance and reduced injuries—rests on analyses that do not hold up under scrutiny. A corrigendum would be required, and the statistical significance of the injury reductions might not survive cluster-adjusted testing.         The findings are real and material. The paper should be corrected or withdrawn.

Let me continue with more reconstruct_2x2 for other survey rows, r_grim for more percentages, chi-square for injury, required_n for power, check_ratio for vitamin C, and GRIM at the rec...The paper's statistical claims are internally inconsistent on multiple levels. The chi-square tests for MSKI (25/80 vs 14/79) and BSI (12/80 vs 4/79) are reported as significant (p=.047 and .037), but the denominators are too small for the observed 25% relative reductions to be credible under any reasonable clustering by flight. With only two clusters per arm, the effective sample size is closer to 4 than 159, and the reported p-values are anti-conservative by construction. The same issue applies to the survey compliance rows: the percentages (14.86% vs 34.25%, 37.84% vs 63.01%, etc.) cannot be produced from n=80 and n=79, and the paper's own completeness statement ("all trainees completed questionnaires") makes the discrepancy glaring. The power analysis claiming n=77 per cohort for a 25% relative increase is 20-fold too small; even at conventional power 0.80 the required n is >1500 for a 25% relative effect at baseline 0.15. The vitamin C entry in Table I is also wrong—100 μg is physiologically implausible (NIH RDA is 85–120 mg), and the printed 83% daily value only matches if the amount is 100 mg. Finally, the age means (21±3 vs 23±5) produce a t-statistic of –3.06 (p=0.0026) that directly contradicts the "no significant difference" claim in the text. These are not 11 independent problems; they are symptoms of a single underlying issue: the analysis was performed on the wrong sample size and then misreported.

Those p-values underpin the abstract's 43% and 66% relative reductions. With two clusters per arm the tests are anti-conservative; a valid cluster analysis is essentially unidentified. Limitation (1) noted block randomization but did not change the analysis.

A title and causal-language correction is warranted; the briefing comparison remains the experiment that was run.

The 66% relative BSI reduction (15% vs 5.06%) is the briefing contrast, not a supplement-versus-placebo effect; both arms received 400 IU vitamin D and 200 mg calcium. Relative to Lappe et al., cited as the dose benchmark, attributing that reduction to a modest compliance increment is a mechanistic-plausibility note, not an arithmetic error in the printed rates.

The omitted survey item n is the same Table III reporting gap already captured by the reconstruct_2x2 finding; the data-availability sentence is a consequence of that gap, not a second defect.

Table I lists vitamin C as 100 μg at 83% daily value. Adjacent rows use μg correctly for vitamins A, D, folate, and B12; 83% matches 100 mg of a 120 mg lactation daily value, not 100 μg. This is a unit typo on a background composition table and does not enter the analyses.

Reconstruct_2x2 finds no n=80/n=79 split that can produce the paired survey percentages; R GRIM finds 14.86% impossible at n=80 and possible at n=74. Recovered bases (11/74, 28/74, 15/74 vs 25/73, 46/73, 6/73; brief items on n=73) also reproduce the printed Pearson p-values. Methods nonetheless state that all trainees completed questionnaires.
verdicts.description: Table III headers are n=80 and n=79 (total 159), but reconstruct_2x2 finds no column split summing to 159 that produces the paired survey percentages (daily MVI 14.86 vs 34.25, most days 37.84 vs 63.01, never 20.27 vs 8.22, found-brief-effective 95.89 vs 98.63). R GRIM agrees 14.86% is impossible at n=80. Unique recovered bases (video compliance 11/74, 28/74, 15/74; in-person 25/73, 46/73, 6/73; brief items on n=73) also reproduce the printed Pearson p-values (.0063, .0023, .037, .007). Methods still state that all trainees completed questionnaires. Compliance contrasts remain; the printed denominators and completeness claim do not.

verdicts.rationale: Methods say alpha 0.05, power 0.99, and a 25% relatively greater daily MVI compliance yielded n=77 per cohort. A two-proportion calculation at those inputs needs thousands per arm for a 25% relative lift from a 0.15 baseline (h≈0.10 → about 3675/group). n=77 per group at 99% power corresponds to a large h≈0.70, which the stated 25% relative change does not produce. The enrolled squadron was not sized by that calculation.

Results state that no significant differences in age were detected. Table II prints 21±3 years (n=80) versus 23±5 (n=79). The implied Cohen's d is −0.48 (95% CI −0.80 to −0.17), which excludes no difference. BMI 24.1±2.6 versus 24.0±2.8 is compatible with the no-difference claim. The age sentence does not match the printed statistics and leaves a two-year imbalance unaddressed in the injury comparison.

The Introduction cites reference 8 for the claim that 27 mg of iron approximates a 22 mg daily requirement for females in military training. Reference 8 as printed is Martineau et al., BMJ 2017, an IPD meta-analysis of vitamin D for acute respiratory infections. Reference 17 (IOM mineral requirements for military personnel) is the work that would bear on that quantity.

The compliance Results paragraph repeats the clause “a significantly higher proportion within the in-person cohort” twice in succession. The following numbers (63.01% vs 37.84%, p=.0023) match Table III. Cosmetic duplication only.

paper.summary: The abstract’s significant MSKI and BSI reductions (p=.047 and p=.037; 43% and 66% relative reductions) are person-level chi-squared tests after randomizing four flights, two per arm. Those p-values match unadjusted Pearson tests on 25/80 versus 14/79 MSKI and 12/80 versus 4/79 BSI. With two clusters per arm the tests are anti-conservative, and a valid cluster analysis is essentially unidentified. Table III survey percentages such as daily MVI 14.86% versus 34.25% cannot be produced from n=80 and n=79; they and the printed p-values match recovered item n of 74 and 73, contrary to the claim that all trainees completed questionnaires. Medical-hold 1.27% is impossible at n=80 (R GRIM). Printed ages 21±3 versus 23±5 contradict the no-difference claim (d=−0.48, CI −0.80 to −0.17). Injury percentages at the stated n, their Pearson p-values, BMI, and the n=80+79 flow do reconcile. The title credits MVI compliance although both arms received the same tablet. A corrigendum should qualify or withdraw the injury significance claims, print survey denominators, and correct the age sentence, medical-hold cell, and title. Nothing here established intent.
